Create a Showback Account

  • A showback account can help with defining a budget amount per project or on a shared basis. The account is used in Creating projects.

    From the main dashboard:

    1. Click Account Management in the left navigation.
    2. Select Showback Accounts.
    3. Click Create Showback Account.
    4. Enter a name for the showback account. Make a note of this name as it will be required as a link in Creating projects.

      A Reference ID is optional. If wanted, use a dummy cost center number.

    5. Provide the following information:

      Budget Type: Per project

      Budget Amount: 500,000

      Recipient Email: user@mail.com

      Keep the default values in the rest of the fields.
    6. Review the summary of the showback account , and then click Create
    The account that you have created will be used as a link in Creating projects.

Create Plans and Pricing

  • As an administrator of the MPC portal, you can:

    • Modify an existing plan
    • Add a new plan
    • Change pricing for various cloud resources such as CPU, memory, and storage.

    From the main dashboard:

    1. Click Services, Managed Private Cloud, Administration, Plans & Pricing.
    2. To modify an existing plan, click the pencil icon to the right of the Medium plan.
    3. Change the CPU to 4, and then click Update.
    4. Click Yes on the Update Plan prompt.
      You have successfully changed the plan.
    5. To add a new plan, scroll down to Add a Plan and click it.
    6. Enter the following information for the new plan:
      CPU:
      16
      Memory:
      64 GB
      Name:
      X Large
    7. Click Add.
      You have successfully added a new plan.
    8. Alternatively, you can delete an existing plan by clicking the X icon on the right side of the existing plan and adding a new plan.
      Note: For the purposes of this demonstration, the deletion is performed but not confirmed on prompting.

    9. Click Cancel.
      Note: If you click Yes, an error displays because this function has not been enabled for the demonstration.

    10. To modify the prices of CPU, memory, or storage, click Edit Pricing.
    11. On this page, you can change the price of any of the cloud resources and then click Submit .
      Note: For this demonstration, click Cancel .

Creating a Showback Report

  • As a FinOps user, you can:

    • Review the showback report
    • View reports by all the projects or a specific project for budgeted amount that is compared with amounts spent
    • Examine a specific project by cost center or resource types such as VMs or clusters

    To create a showback report:

    1. Click Services > Reporting > Cost > Showback Report.
      By default, the Showback Report page displays Budget versus Actual Spend data for all projects. The top section of the report displays the Cost Summary, while the bottom section displays Top Spend By Projects and Top Spend By Resource Types.
    2. Under Showback Report, click the Showback Account drop-down and select Demo Test Showback account .
    3. Take a few moments to review the displayed data.
    4. Click View All Spends under each Top Spends section and review the data.
    5. Click the Export button to download the report for further integration.

Creating projects

  • As as an administrator of the Managed Private Cloud portal, you can:
    • Create a project,
    • Assign a showback account to the project
    • Add users and roles to the project

    To create a project:

    1. Continuing from Roles, User Group, Users, locate Account Management in the left navigation and click Projects.
    2. Click Create Project.
    3. On the page that opens, enter the following details:
      Name:
      Desired name of the project
      Showback Account:
      Select the showback account that you created in Create a Showback Account.

      Click Continue.

    4. On the next page that opens, click Add User for Project Membership.

      A drawer opens on the right side of the page containing the option to add a user:

    5. . Select the user that you created in Creating Roles, User Groups, and Users .
    6. Click Continue as an administrator of the Managed Private Cloud portal.
    7. Select the role that you created in Creating Roles, User Groups, and Users and click Add, and then click Continue.
    8. Review the Create Project page, and then click Create.
      You are prompted to confirm that you want to create the project.
    9. Click Yes.
    You have successfully created the project and assigned users to it.

Creating Roles, User Groups, and Users

  • As an administrator of the Managed Private Cloud portal , you can create a custom role, user group, and a user, and then assign the custom role to the user.

    From the main dashboard:

    1. Click User Management in the left navigation and select Roles.
    2. Enter the following details:
      Role Name:
      Name of your choice
      Description:
      Short description of the new role
      Assign Permissions:
      Enter the word network in the search field.
      Assigned:
      Select the Administer Networkcheck box.
    3. Click Create.
      The new custom role is created.
    4. From User Management in the left navigation, click User Groups.
    5. Click Create User Group.
    6. Enter the following details:
      Name:
      Name of your choice
      Description:
      Short description of the user group
    7. Assign the role that you created in ABC Network Admin and click Continue.
    8. Assign a user.

      To do this, click the checkbox next to a username in the list and click Create.

    9. In User Management in the left navigation, click Users.
      The user group is created.
    10. In User Management in the left navigation, click Users and click Create User.
    11. Enter the user Email Address you want to add.
    12. Under Assign User Group, search for the user group you created earlier by typing the first few characters of the group name in the search field. Select the group and click Create.
      You have added the user to the Managed Private Cloud portal.

Document purpose

  • This guide provides configuration details for implementing Managed Private Cloud on Dell PowerFlex compute and storage. It also demonstrates how to use the Managed Private Cloud capabilities in a PowerFlex and VMware Hypervisor environment.

    Managed Private Cloud is designed to operate on different hardware types and configurations. For this reason, guidelines for deploying and configuring the physical compute, storage, and network devices are outside the scope of this document.

    Note: This guide provides examples of how to perform various VMware vSphere activities using PowerFlex systems and Dell software. These examples were developed for laboratory testing and may need adjusting to suit other operational environments. Ensure that any procedures that are outlined in this guide are thoroughly tested before implementing them in a production environment. For information about updated configurations for newer software and hardware versions, contact your Dell Technologies sales representative.

    Audience

    This document is intended for cloud administrators, system administrators, and VMware vSphere administrators and developers.

    Readers of this document are expected to be familiar with:

    • PowerFlex system operation
    • Dell software including PowerFlex Manager (4.x)
    • General storage concepts
    • VMware Cloud Foundation, including vSphere, NSX, and vSAN
    • VMware vSphereproducts and their operations
      Note: Images from both VCF 5.1.1 and VCF 5.2 are present.

      Note: Users are expected to be familiar with the products and technologies that this guide describes, and therefore not every step of each wizard walkthrough has an associated image. The corresponding steps are always documented, however.

    Table 1. Revision History

Executive summary

  • Managed Private Cloud is an API-driven solution that aims to provide a public cloud-like experience on-premises, enabling IT administrators, system engineers, and developers to deploy workloads and applications using a unified self-service portal. This experience increases visibility, operational efficiency, and development velocity by enabling Infrastructure as a Code (IaC).

    Managed Private Cloud brings the best of private and public cloud benefits to your workloads, providing the following benefits to internal and external customers alike:

    • The highest level of abstraction that improves cloud consumer experience productivity by lowering development complexity and providing higher operational efficiency.
    • A vendor-agnostic multicloud solution that provides a seamless experience across the cloud for customers, enabling a game-changing end-to-end software development experience.

    Managed Private Cloud is a capability within Dell Managed Services Platform (DMSP). Managed Private Cloud also has other capabilities, as described in this guide, and as part of the Dell Technologies managed services offering.

    Dell PowerFlex is a software-defined infrastructure that is designed to reduce operational and infrastructure complexity, empowering organizations to move faster by delivering flexibility, elasticity, and simplicity with predictable performance and resiliency at scale. The PowerFlex family provides a foundation that combines compute and high-performance storage resources in a managed, unified fabric.

    Note: PowerFlex does not support VMware Virtual Volumes with PowerFlex 4.x and is therefore not an available option for VCF storage.

Image Management

  • As an administrator of the Managed Private Cloud portal, you can publish images to be used for VM or container cluster provisioning.
    1. Under Administration, click Image Management.
    2. Under All Images on the right, click AAP2.
    3. Enter a name that you want to provide to your image, for example, ABCImage.
      For this laboratory exercise, skip the description and logo image .
    4. Enter the following details:
      Version
      1
      Category:
      OS
      Sub Category
      Nginx
      Price:
      15
    5. Click Publish.
    6. To make changes to an existing published image, click Ubuntu.
      Notice the various properties of the image and the list of instances that are provisioned using this image:
    7. Click Edit.
      A page opens that is similar to the page that displayed when you published a new image.
    8. Make your changes and click Update.
      Note: For this demonstration exercise, click Cancel .

    9. On the Cancel changes prompt, click Yes.

Introduction

  • Dell Managed Services Platform

    Customer experience with Dell Managed Services Platform

    Dell Technologies Managed Services (DTMS) enhances the customer experience in cloud technology deployment through Dell Managed Services Platform (DMSP), which offers tools and capabilities along with a new operating model. This model addresses four key transformation areas: the modern workforce experience, data applications, cloud platforms, and business resiliency. DMSP supports DTMS with provisioning services, life cycle updating, integrated incident and change management, security and compliance, cost management, and maintaining availability. Using automation, standardization, and security, DMSP provides a self-service platform that aligns with industry best practices, resulting in a more intuitive and seamless experience. Security is a fundamental aspect, ensuring consistent administration and better customer insight into cloud technology transformation.

Introduction

  • Customer Logical Infrastructure Configuration requirements

    VMWare vSphere requirements

    To enable Managed Private Cloud, provide the following information to Dell Technologies:

    1. A vCenter Service Account for Managed Private Cloud. The account should have administrator-level permissions.
    2. A provisioned datastore or datastores with available capacity to support calculated provisioning needs (the average storage size X number of VMs expected + 2 TB buffer is recommended).
    3. A vCenter appliance API URL and IP address

    VMWare NSX-T Requirements

    Provide the following information to Dell Technologies:

    • An NSX-T Manager API URL and IP address
    • A list of the local subnets to be used.
    • An NSX-T Service Account. The account should have administrator-level permissions.
    • Configured Ingress/Egress routing.
    Note: Guidelines for deploying and configuring vCenter, NSX-T, and the related VMware ESXi environment are outside of the scope of this document.

Managed Private Cloud deployment options

  • To cater to diverse business needs, Managed Private Cloud offers Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) and on-premises deployment models. :

    SaaS model:

    This model provides:

    • New features through continuous software delivery
    • Elastic scalability
    • Dell is responsible for:
      • Maintaining the platform
      • The security of the platform in the Cloud

    On-Premises model:

    This model is hosted alongside customer infrastructure.

    • The customer is responsible for the security and compliance of the platform infrastructure
    • New feature rollout requires manual intervention

    SaaS Deployment Model

    To enable delivery of the Managed Private Cloud solution from the Dell SaaS platform, connectivity to your premises is required from the Dell remote management zone (RMZ) in Microsoft Azure. Each RMZ is customer-specific and has no connectivity to or from any other RMZ.

    The preferred RMZ connectivity method is a site-to-site VPN tunnel. However, if you have an existing Azure Express Route that you want to use, inform Dell Technologies of this preference in an architectural workshop. You will be required to provide an Express Route Authorization key to enable the Dell RMZ to use your express route.

    Regardless of the connectivity method used, you must ensure that traffic from the Dell RMZ can reach the management networks containing any vCenter, and NSX-T APIs that are being used with Managed Private Cloud, as well as the networks containing the ESXi hosts. Connectivity to the ESXi hosts is required to provide developers with console access to the VMs deployed using Managed Private Cloud.

    On-Premises Deployment Model

    Ensure that:

    • The physical PowerFlex hardware resources are deployed:
    • On-premises in place of cloud is available locally using the Ansible-Kubernetes framework.
    • All the required code has been developed and checked in to the GIT repository.

    The environment can be pulled locally into the systems where the Managed Private Cloud is to be deployed. Appropriate changes will be implemented.

    Customer Details

    The following customer details are required for setting up the inventory for a Managed Private Cloud on-premises deployment. These details must be available before the deployment:

    • keycloak_realm_name
    • vCenter Details:
      • Host name
      • User name
      • Password
      • resource_pool
    • NSX Details:
      • nsx_url
      • nsx_user
      • nsx_password
    • NSX AVI Details:
      • nsx_avi_url
      • nsx_avi_user
      • nsx_avi_password
    • public_site_url
    • initial_user_email

Overview

  • Launch a Virtual Machine

    Perform the following steps:

    1. In the left navigation, click Services.
    2. Click Managed Private Cloud > Virtualization Service.
    3. In the upper right corner, click Launch New Instance.
    4. Provide the following input:
      Instance Name:
      The name that you want to give your VM.
      Project Name:
      Select Demo TEST Project.
      Environment:
      Select Development.
      Data Center:
      Select Dallas, TX.
      The page that opens shows the values that you have entered:
    5. Click Instances.
    6. Scroll down to Browse Catalog and click it.
    7. Select the Ubuntu image, as shown in the preceding figure.
    8. Under Plan Storage, leave Pre-configured Plans selected and choose Medium from the drop-down menu.
    9. Click Add Storage, double-click the Size (GB) field, and enter 50.
    10. In the upper right corner, under Cost Summary, click Cost Breakdown to view various cloud resources costs. Click Continue.
    11. Click the Network and select dc02.segment.
    12. Under Security Group, select Create New and enter the name of your security group.
    13. Under Firewall Rules, click Add Rules.
    14. Enter Inbound Rules, and then enter Outbound Rules.
    15. Click Save and proceed to review the firewall rules.
    16. Click Continue.
    17. Click Deploy Instance.

      The newly deployed VM is listed under Instances with its current status showing as Running.

Overview

  • VM Dashboard and Day 2 Actions

    You can perform the following Day 2 actions on VMs using the Managed Private Cloud:
    • View the utilization of CPU, memory, network, attached resources such as storage, firewall, and security groups, and a historical log of actions performed on the VM.
    • Shut down and start the VM.
    • Take snapshots of the VM.
    1. Click Instances.
      The list of instances opens.
    2. Click Internet Test.
    3. In the Details section under Utilization, click CPU, Memory, or Network as required to view the associated utilization details.
      The View option on the right provides more granular details: today, last 7 days, last month.
      Note: For this demonstration, the data for last 7 days and last month is not available.

    4. Click Instances, and then click AK_test.
    5. Take a few minutes to review the following tabs under Details: Storage, Network, Snapshots, History..
    6. Click More Actions, Resize and select Medium from the drop-down menu.
    7. Click Update. and observe the VM state change first to Resizing and then back to Running while it applies the configuration changes.
    8. Go to the Snapshots tab and make a note of existing snapshots. Click Snapshot.
    9. Enter a name for the snapshot and click Create.

      Notice that the new snapshot is created instantly.

    10. On the same test VM, try to stop and start the VM. To do this, click Stop VM first, and then click Proceed.

      Notice that the status changes to Stopping.

    11. Click Start VM, and then click Proceed.

      Notice that the status changes to Starting first and then to Running.

    12. Click the arrow that is displayed in the page that opens to view the Internet test.

Performance Test Results

  • Conclusion

    The tests simulated a range of user loads, starting with 8 users and scaling up to 128 users. In each test scenario, users performed everyday tasks such as VM provisioning, data retrieval, and application deployment as quickly as possible.

    Key performance metrics, including Average Requests per Second (RPS), various response times, and response time stability, were captured to provide a comprehensive view of system performance. The increased response times suggest that the Managed Private Cloud system can handle the load. The bottleneck appears to be the size of the vCenter used as part of the test environment.

    The performance test setup for Managed Private Cloud using PowerFlex was designed to rigorously evaluate the system's ability to handle different user loads. By capturing key metrics, the testing team aimed to identify potential bottlenecks and ensure the system's robustness and scalability.

    Note: Locust workers are Python processes, and each user within these processes is a Python thread. These threads operate much faster than real users, which means that 128 Locust users can simulate the activity of thousands of real users.

Performance Tests

  • Managed Private Cloud Performance Test for Using PowerFlex

    The Managed Private Cloud powered by PowerFlex is designed for high performance, scalability, and resilience. To ensure that the system can meet enterprise demands, the Dell PowerFlex team conducted comprehensive performance tests on the system. The tests evaluated ability to handle various user loads and identify potential bottlenecks.

    The tests were meticulously planned and performed on an 8-core VM on a management server outside the cluster, ensuring no interference with cluster performance. The proximity of the VM to the target system minimized network hops and latency. The testing team used Locust.io, configured with 8 worker processes, for load testing. Locust.io is an open-source, Python-based load testing tool that allows developers to simulate thousands or even millions of concurrent users accessing a system, helping identify performance bottlenecks and ensure scalability. For more information, see Locust.io.

    Objective

    The Managed Private Cloud Performance Test for Using PowerFlex evaluates the ability of the system to handle various user loads and identify potential bottlenecks. The testing simulated different user loads and tasks, such as VM provisioning, data retrieval, and application deployment, to assess the system's performance under varying conditions.

    System Setup

    The configuration is a small test environment. This in no way depicts the production configuration and is not intended as guidance for planning your sizing activities.

    Testing Environment

    The PowerFlext team conducted the tests on a VM located on a management server outside the cluster being tested. This configuration ensures that the management server does not interfere with the performance of the cluster.
    Testing environment:
    The performance tests were conducted on a VM located on a management server outside the cluster being tested. This configuration ensures that the management server does not interfere with the performance of the cluster.
    vCenter Server:
    8vCPU, 30 GB RAM, 17 Hard Disks, VMXNET3 Network Adapter
    Managed Private Cloud:
    12vCPU, 16 GB Ram, 300 GB Disk, E1000E
    Locust VM specifications:
    The testing VM was equipped with 8 cores to handle the load efficiently.
    Load testing tool:
    For load testing, the team used Locust.io configured with 8 worker processes, each corresponding to one system core.
    Network configuration:
    The VM was positioned close to the target system to minimize network hops, ensuring optimal communication and reducing latency.

    Testing Methodology

    User simulation:
    Each test simulated a varying number of users (8, 16, 24, 32, and 128) performing everyday tasks against the system as rapidly as possible. These tasks included VM provisioning, data retrieval, and application deployment.
    Initial fluctuations:
    Most tests exhibited fluctuations at the start, probably because of to the influx of VM provisioning requests required for a large number of operations.

    Data Captured

    Average Requests per Second (RPS):
    This metric measures the average number of requests that the system handles per second, providing insight into throughput.
    Response times:
    Various response times were recorded to evaluate the speed and efficiency of the system in handling user requests.
    Response time stability:
    The testing team measured the stability of response times to identify any inconsistencies or performance degradation over time.

    Disclaimer

    The testing and performance evaluations described in this white paper were conducted in a controlled test environment using Dell PowerFlex as part of a Managed Private Cloud deployment. These results are intended for informational purposes only. Actual performance and outcomes in a production environment may vary significantly depending on specific hardware configurations, virtual infrastructure, workload characteristics, and other environmental factors. Organizations should conduct their own testing and validation to ensure suitability for their unique operational requirements.

PowerFlex Family

  • PowerFlex software-defined infrastructure enables broad consolidation across the data center, encompassing most workloads. The software-first architecture enables automation and programmability of the complete infrastructure stack. PowerFlex provides scalability, performance, and resiliency to enable effortless adherence to stringent workload SLAs.

    The PowerFlex family provides a foundation that combines compute and high-performance storage resources in a managed unified fabric. PowerFlex comes in flexible consumption options (rack, appliance, custom nodes, or in the public cloud) that enable independent (disaggregated) architectures. PowerFlex is ideal for high-performance applications and databases, building an agile private/hybrid cloud, or consolidating resources in heterogeneous environments.

    PowerFlex software components

    Software is the key differentiation in the PowerFlex offering. PowerFlex software components not only provide the distributed software-defined storage services but also help simplify infrastructure management and orchestration. The management software enables comprehensive IT Operational Management (ITOM) and Life Cycle Management (LCM) capabilities that span compute as well as storage infrastructure, from BIOS and Firmware to nodes, software, and networking.

    PowerFlex core software

    PowerFlex is a software-defined scale-out block storage service that is designed to deliver flexibility, elasticity, and simplicity with predictable high performance and resiliency at scale.

    For more details, see PowerFlex specifications.

    PowerFlex Manager

    PowerFlex Manager enables ITOM automation and LCM capabilities for PowerFlex systems. The unified PowerFlex Manager brings together three separate components used in previous releases – PowerFlex Manager, the core PowerFlex UI, and the PowerFlex gateway. The PowerFlex UI runs in Kubernetes and embraces a modern development framework.

PowerFlex Family

  • PowerFlex deployment architectures

    PowerFlex software-defined storage can be deployed in disaggregated architectures, that is, with independent compute and storage layers.

    Independent architecture

    In an independent or disaggregated architecture, some nodes provide storage capacity for data in applications, while other separate and independent nodes provide compute resources for applications and workloads. Compute and storage resources can be scaled independently by adding nodes to the cluster while it remains active. This separation of compute and storage resources helps minimize software licensing costs in certain situations. This architecture can be ideal for high-performance databases and application workloads.

    Disaggregation gives organizations the freedom to choose different LCM options that best align with their operational models. Not only can PowerFlex Manager manage the LCM of the PowerFlex storage infrastructure, it can also manage LCM of PowerFlex compute nodes. With this freedom there is also the choice to manage compute estates that connect to PowerFlex with other tooling; for example, VxRail Dynamic Nodes connected to PowerFlex using VxRail Manager automation.

PowerFlex Family

  • PowerFlex consumption options

    PowerFlex rack

    PowerFlex rack is a software-defined infrastructure platform that combines compute as well as high-performance storage resources in a managed unified network. This rack-based engineered system, with integrated networking, enables customers to achieve the scalability and management requirements of a modern data center.

    PowerFlex appliance

    PowerFlex appliance is a PowerEdge-based server which has been configured to be a node in a software-defined storage deployment that runs PowerFlex software components. This offering allows customers the flexibility and savings to bring their own compatible networking or make use of full network automation using a supported set of Dell or Cisco switches.

    PowerFlex custom nodes

    PowerFlex Custom Nodes are validated server building-blocks configured for use with PowerFlex. They are available with thousands of configuration options and are available for customers who prefer to build their own environments.

    PowerFlex in the public cloud

    PowerFlex software storage services can be deployed on recommended instances (with attached storage) in Amazon Web Services or Microsoft Azure. Only the MG data layout and Independent (disaggregated) architecture is supported. Fault Sets may be used to distribute the cluster across multiple Availability Zones (AZs), improving resiliency even during AZ disruptions. Native asynchronous replication may be used to migrate data between cloud and on-premises PowerFlex systems, or to establish cloud-based BC/DR data protection schemes.

    PowerFlex CSI/CSM 

    An important component outside of PowerFlex that enables a flexible consumption model for Kubernetes is the PowerFlex CSI driver, developed as a part of the Dell Kubernetes strategy. After lthe CSI driver for PowerFlex is loaded into Kubernetes, it can be used to provision persistent volumes from the underlying PowerFlex storage resource. If the Kubernetes deployment is running low on PowerFlex storage resources, you can add PowerFlex storage nodes to increase the system capacity and performance.

    The CSI driver connects the PowerFlex system and Kubernetes deployments. It is a storage broker which dynamically provisions volumes from PowerFlex through the PowerFlex API gateway to the Kubernetes cluster. Once the volume is available on PowerFlex, it is immediately mapped to the requesting pod. If a pod is destroyed or rescheduled, the CSI plug-in ensures that the volumes are remapped upon rescheduling of that pod. 

    • Customers running Kubernetes clusters on PowerFlex use the Dell Container Storage Modules (CSM), which extend the CSI driver capabilities. These modules:
    • Provide enterprise storage capabilities to Kubernetes for cloud-native stateful applications.
    • Reduce management complexity, so that developers can independently use enterprise storage with ease and automate daily operations.
    • Extends storage functionality and capabilities beyond using the CSI driver alone.

    These modules include replication, observability, authorization, application mobility, and resiliency.

VMware Hypervisor

  • Dell Managed Private Cloud leverages a VMware Hypervisor stack consisting of VMware vSphere, VMware NSXT, and VMware vSAN. These three components serve the following roles:

    • SDDC Manager: Automates the life cycle management of VCF. SDDC Manager enables updating and upgrades, firmware application, and the general day-to-day operation of VCF.
    • VMware vSphere: Virtualizes the bare-metal servers using the ESXi software and aggregates them in the vCenter server.
    • VMware NSXData Center: Provides the networking for the VCF solution along with security and automation. NSX is designed for both private and public clouds.
